name: Taíno and Caribbean peoples
summary: The peoples of the Caribbean islands, especially the Taíno of the Greater Antilles, the first Americans to meet Columbus in 1492. Their population collapsed under Spanish rule.

knownFor.label: Batey ball game
knownFor.note: A ball game played on courts.

location.value: Most of the West Indies, from the Bahamas through the Greater Antilles to Guadeloupe in the northern Lesser Antilles.

terrain.value: Islands with mountains, forests and coasts.

climate.value: Tropical, with a hurricane season from June to November.

resources.value: Cassava, sweet potatoes, fish and cotton.

disasters.value: Hurricanes (a Taíno word) struck the islands regularly.

population.value: Pre-1492 estimates for Hispaniola range from 10,000 to 1,000,000; a 2020 genetic analysis suggests no more than a few tens of thousands.

urbanisation.value: Villages of a few hundred to a few thousand.

disease.value: European diseases killed most Taíno after 1492.

migration.value: Arawakan peoples arrived from South America.

economicBase.value: Cassava (yuca) grown in raised mounds (conucos) was the staple, followed by sweet potato; maize, squash, beans, peppers, peanuts and pineapples were also grown, with fishing and hunting.

tradeRoutes.value: Canoes carried goods and people between islands and to the South American coast.

wealth.value: No estimate is possible; gold was used for ornaments, not money.

moneyAndTax.value: No money; chiefs received tribute in food and goods.

governmentType.value: Villages were ruled by a cacique (or cacica) and chiefdoms (cacicazgos) could form a confederation; chiefs generally gained power through the maternal line. There were four classes: cacique, nitaínos, bohíques (priests) and naborias (workers).

keyRulers.value: Hatuey fled to Cuba to unite its people and was burned at the stake on 2 February 1512. Enriquillo led more than 3,000 Taíno in a successful rebellion on Hispaniola in the 1520s. Anacaona and Guarionex are not covered in the part of the page read.

succession.value: Chiefs (caciques) often inherited through the mother’s line.

institutions.value: Councils of nobles and religious specialists, led by caciques.

stability.value: Rivalry between chiefdoms, but also long periods of peace.

eliteConflict.value: Not well recorded; Spanish accounts mention rivalries between caciques.

armyAndTech.value: Wooden clubs and bows, and war canoes.

majorWars.value: Hatuey was burned at the stake on 2 February 1512; Enriquillo led a successful rebellion on Hispaniola in the 1520s.

territoryChange.value: They lost their islands to Spain after 1492.

alliancesRivals.value: Chiefdoms formed alliances by marriage; the Kalinago raided Taíno islands.

inventions.value: Hammocks, dugout canoes and cassava processing.

scienceEducation.value: Oral knowledge of plants, stars and the sea.

openness.value: Welcomed Columbus at first; resistance grew as the Spanish enslaved people.

communicationTransport.value: Dugout canoes carried people and goods between islands.

religion.value: Worship centred on zemis (spirits or ancestors); the major zemis were Atabey and her son Yúcahu.

languageWriting.value: Taíno (Arawakan); words like hurricane, canoe, barbecue.

artsArchitecture.value: Carved zemí figures, ball courts and stone plazas.

sharedIdentity.value: A shared language, ball game and zemí religion across the islands.

dailyLife.value: Round houses (bohío) of wood and thatch; cassava bread, fish.

neighbours.value: The Kalinago (Island Caribs) in the Lesser Antilles.

ideasReligions.value: Spanish rule forced Christianity, though some Taíno beliefs survived.

colonisation.value: Colonised by Spain from 1492; their numbers fell sharply from disease and forced labour.

riseSignals.value: DNA studies link the Taíno to pottery-making farmers who entered the Caribbean from north-eastern South America about 2,500 years ago.

peakPeriod.value: About 1200–1500, when large chiefdoms existed on Hispaniola.

declineSignals.value: Columbus landed in the Bahamas on 12 October 1492; forced labour under the encomienda and infectious disease followed; famine in 1495–96 reportedly killed about 50,000.

outcome.value: 80–90% of the Taíno died within 30 years of contact, mostly from disease; Spanish documents declared them extinct as early as 1550.
